[[:db/retract 17592186152792 :question/answer-fields 17592186151259] {:db/id 17592186152097 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-e91f8fe9-c6f2-558a-bf39-b0389019d5ff" "question-44e36839-2675-57c4-abf9-91a0b0717003" "question-abd84654-ac2d-58a6-9574-529f2b4aa6f5" "question-a55de8de-5dbf-5007-a3cb-517652d485f3"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186151846 :question/problem "Which of the following integers belong to the residue class $[5]_{8}?$

- $-3$

- $13$

- $3$" :question/worked-solution "The residue class $[5]_{8}$ consists of the elements that are congruent to $5$ modulo $8.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}[5]_{8} & ={x\in Z\,|\,x≡5\,(\text{mod}\,8)} \\  & ={x\in Z\,|\,x=5+8k,\,k\in Z} \\  & ={5+8k\,|\,k\in Z} \\  & ={…,\,5-2\cdot 8,\,5-8,\,5,\,5+8,\,5+2\cdot 8,\,…} \\  & ={…,-11,-3,5,13,21,…}.\end{aligned}
$$

We see that $-3$ and $13$ belong to $[5]_{8},$ while $3$ does not.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186152098 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-4eec4737-7c33-5f5e-94da-8528e3f19d9b" "question-9486abbb-c811-54ba-bf39-16141b4e8ba4" "question-476816fb-a049-55c8-86b3-04683cf8a95e" "question-9c32efaa-b6d9-5d28-a23f-80c818eab9ef" "question-d1a9f6cf-cd8d-55d6-a82c-4176e7807557"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186151847 :question/problem "Which of the following residue classes modulo $3$ contain the integer $7?$

- $[4]_3$

- $[-1]_3$

- $[1]_3$" :question/worked-solution "We have $7 \in [a]_{3}$ if 

$$
7 \equiv a \quad (\text{mod}\:3).
$$

Let's now consider each of the given equivalence classes.

- $7 \in [4]_3$ because $7 \equiv 4 \: (\text{mod}\:3)$ $\quad \color{green}\checkmark$

- $7 \not\in [-1]_3$ because $7 \not\equiv -1 \: (\text{mod}\:3)$ $\quad \color{red}\times$

- $7 \in [1]_3$ because $7 \equiv 1 \: (\text{mod}\:3)$ $\quad \color{green}\checkmark$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186152099 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-6ec8e64f-343c-590b-a372-9757c285ca4e" "question-c46ee0cd-65d1-59a8-92bc-e1fc2e8dbb10" "question-0c2846ce-57fa-59ad-9fe2-ab1c6ed9c653" "question-1bd78006-ade4-5556-a33a-5b5262685fbe" "question-06e706ec-ef55-5e4d-a1fb-e7ced3a44078"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186151848 :question/problem "If $[a]_n$ denotes the residue class containing all integers congruent to $a$ modulo $n,$ then which of the following residue classes is equal to $[13]_3?$

- $[0]_3$

- $[1]_3$

- $[2]_3$" :question/worked-solution "We have $[a]_{3} = [b]_{3}$ if 

$$
a \equiv b \quad (\text{mod}\:3).
$$

The residue class $[13]_{3}$ consists of the elements that are congruent to $13$ modulo $3.$ 

We can find an alternative representation for this residue class as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[13]_{3} & ={x\in Z\,|\,x≡13\,(\text{mod}\,3)} \\  & ={x\in Z\,|\,x≡4\cdot 3+1\,(\text{mod}\,3)} \\  & ={x\in Z\,|\,x≡4\cdot 0+1\,(\text{mod}\,3)} \\  & ={x\in Z\,|\,x≡1\,(\text{mod}\,3)} \\  & =[1]_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only"." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186152100 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-f68491fc-7fbf-551d-bb56-21bac80c159f" "question-0f9012f2-83ba-5f6f-b553-2ea47d5d4f81" "question-b83f0a5d-69e2-5527-92eb-107f538fccca" "question-32f1fbfd-ebfc-5a37-bf9e-b69da2b29724" "question-82a421fb-21ef-5dca-a27b-abed22994846"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186151850 :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true?

- There are $4$ distinct residue classes modulo $8$

- $[5]_{3} \cap [9]_{3} = \emptyset$

- $\mathbb{Z} = [4]_{3} \cup [5]_{3} \cup [9]_{3}$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the residue classes modulo $n$ have the following properties:

- There are exactly $n$ distinct residue classes modulo $n$

- Two distinct residue classes have an empty intersection: $[a]_n \cap [b]_n = \emptyset$ if $a \not\equiv b \: (\text{mod}\:n)$

- Residue classes modulo $n$ form a partition of the set of all integers: 

$$
\mathbb{Z} = [0]_n \cup [1]_n \cup \cdots \cup [n-1]_n
$$

- The integers modulo $n$ is defined as the set containing all distinct residue classes modulo $n$: 

$$
\mathbb{Z}_n = \big\{[0]_n,\, [1]_n,\, \ldots,\,  [n-1]_n\big\}
$$

With that in mind, let's now consider each of the given statements.

- Statement I is false. There are exactly $8$ distinct residue classes modulo $8.$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, since $5 \not\equiv 9 \: (\text{mod }3),$ we have that $[5]_3\cap [9]_3= \emptyset.$

- Statement III is true. First, notice the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}[4]_{3} & =[1+3\cdot 1]_{3}=[1]_{3} \\ [5]_{3} & =[2+3\cdot 1]_{3}=[2]_{3} \\ [9]_{3} & =[0+3\cdot 3]_{3}=[0]_{3}\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}[4]_{3}\cup [5]_{3}\cup [9]_{3} & =[1]_{3}\cup [2]_{3}\cup [0]_{3} \\  & =[0]_{3}\cup [1]_{3}\cup [2]_{3} \\  & =Z.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only"." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-e91f8fe9-c6f2-558a-bf39-b0389019d5ff" :question/id #uuid "e91f8fe9-c6f2-558a-bf39-b0389019d5ff" :question/math-academy-id "q-86021" :question/problem "Which of the following integers belong to the residue class $[7]_{11}?$

- $18$
- $-4$
- $15$" :question/worked-solution "The residue class $[7]_{11}$ consists of the elements that are congruent to $7$ modulo $11.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}[7]_{11} & ={x\in Z\,|\,x≡7\,(\text{mod}\,11)} \\  & ={x\in Z\,|\,x=7+11k,\,k\in Z} \\  & ={7+11k\,|\,k\in Z} \\  & ={…,\,7-2\cdot 11,\,7-11,\,7,\,7+11,\,7+2\cdot 11,…} \\  & ={…,-15,-4,7,18,29,…}.\end{aligned}
$$

We see that $-4$ and $18$ belong to $[7]_{11},$ while $15$ does not.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only"." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-f2e9f81c-9578-565c-8322-3231a43ad273"] :db/ensure - There are $11$ distinct residue classes modulo $11$
- $[7]_{5}\cap [2]_{5}\ne ∅$
- $Z=[0]_{4}\cup [9]_{4}\cup [2]_{4}\cup [15]_{4}$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the residue classes modulo $n$ have the following properties:

- There are exactly $n$ distinct residue classes modulo $n$

- Two distinct residue classes have an empty intersection: $[a]_{n}\cap [b]_{n}=∅$ if $a≢b\,(\text{mod}\,n)$

- Residue classes modulo $n$ form a partition of the set of all integers: 

$$
Z=[0]_{n}\cup [1]_{n}\cup ⋯\cup [n-1]_{n}
$$

- The integers modulo $n$ is defined as the set containing all distinct residue classes modulo $n$: 

$$
{Z}_{n}={[0]_{n},\,[1]_{n},\,…,\,[n-1]_{n}}
$$

With that in mind, let's now consider each of the given statements.

- Statement I is true. There are $11$ distinct residue classes modulo $11.$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, since $7≡2\,(\text{mod }5),$ we have that $[7]_{5}=[2]_{5}.$ Therefore, $[7]_{5}\cap [2]_{5}\ne ∅.$

- Statement III is true. First, notice the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}[9]_{4} & =[1+4\cdot 2]_{4}=[1]_{4} \\ [15]_{4} & =[3+4\cdot 3]_{4}=[3]_{4}\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}[0]_{4}\cup [9]_{4}\cup [2]_{4}\cup [15]_{4} & =[0]_{4}\cup [1]_{4}\cup [2]_{4}\cup [3]_{4} \\  & =Z\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III"." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-0dd3a9af-e1c5-54e0-8441-f550817b9384"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-0dd3a9af-e1c5-54e0-8441-f550817b9384" :answer-field/id #uuid "0dd3a9af-e1c5-54e0-8441-f550817b9384" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-ccfb74cf-ee0e-514f-afc8-cbb35b8f9393" :answer-field/choices ["answer-52eadcaf-a11c-568b-907e-2ff81396dc49" "answer-406d20f8-1407-5435-8784-5f3e29ff681c" "answer-7ecfdc45-6d9f-55e1-936c-36ea7836a224" "answer-ccfb74cf-ee0e-514f-afc8-cbb35b8f9393" "answer-4a92891f-39e5-5cee-b46a-8784882f23fc"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-52eadcaf-a11c-568b-907e-2ff81396dc49" :answer/id #uuid "52eadcaf-a11c-568b-907e-2ff81396dc49" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-406d20f8-1407-5435-8784-5f3e29ff681c" :answer/id #uuid "406d20f8-1407-5435-8784-5f3e29ff681c" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7ecfdc45-6d9f-55e1-936c-36ea7836a224" :answer/id #uuid "7ecfdc45-6d9f-55e1-936c-36ea7836a224" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ccfb74cf-ee0e-514f-afc8-cbb35b8f9393" :answer/id #uuid "ccfb74cf-ee0e-514f-afc8-cbb35b8f9393" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I, II, and III" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4a92891f-39e5-5cee-b46a-8784882f23fc" :answer/id #uuid "4a92891f-39e5-5cee-b46a-8784882f23fc" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-0f9012f2-83ba-5f6f-b553-2ea47d5d4f81" :question/id #uuid "0f9012f2-83ba-5f6f-b553-2ea47d5d4f81" :question/math-academy-id "q-78640" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true?

"{[0]_{11},[1]_{11},…,[10]_{11}}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186153456 :tutorial/content "Given an integer $a,$ the **residue class** (or **congruence class**) of $a$ modulo $n$ is the set containing all integers congruent to $a$ (modulo $n$). 

The residue class of $a$ modulo $n,$ denoted $[a]_n,$ can be expressed using a conditional definition as follows:

$$
[a]_n = \big\{ x \in \mathbb{Z} \: | \: x \equiv a \,  \: (\text{mod}\:n) \big\}
$$

Put another way, the residue class $[a]_n$ contains all integers that have the same remainder as $a$ when divided by $n.$

For example, the residue class of $0$ modulo $2$ contains all the even integers because they all have a remainder of zero when divided by $2.$

$$
\begin{aligned}[0]_{2} & ={x\in Z\,|\,x≡0\,(\text{mod}\,2)} \\  & ={2k\,|\,k\in Z} \\  & ={…,-4,-2,0,2,4…}\end{aligned}
$$

The residue class of $1$ modulo $2$ contains all the odd integers because they all have a remainder of one when divided by $2.$

$$
\begin{aligned}[1]_{2} & ={x\in Z\,|\,x≡1\,(\text{mod}\,2)} \\  & ={2k+1\,|\,k\in Z} \\  & ={…,-3,-1,1,3,5…}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that each element of $\mathbb Z$ lies either in $[0]_2$ or in $[1]_2$ (but never both). Thus, these residue classes form a *partition* of the integers. We'll call this partition $\mathbb Z_2{:}$

$$
\mathbb Z_2 = \big\{[0]_2, [1]_2\big\}
$$

We can visualize this partition using the diagram shown below.

![](images/f8/f84b296319e078df1827fe29dbd15fb61ce0d10cac69660f11d6a96d5c44478a.png)

Similarly, the integers can also be partitioned into five residue classes modulo $5.$ 

$$
\mathbb Z_5 = \big\{[0]_5, [1]_5, [2]_5,[3]_5, [4]_5 \big\}
$$

In this case, each residue class contains all numbers that are congruent modulo $5.$ We can visualize this partition of $\mathbb Z$ using the diagram below.

![](images/27/270f63afd4a0022e9f31a48e5ea5f4e799822e8c4eb5813e6c5e616e316c02e1.png)

A residue class is a specific type of a more general object called an **equivalence class.** We'll learn more about different types of equivalence classes soon." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186153479 :tutorial/content "Let's go back to our diagram for visualizing the residue classes modulo ![](images/27/270d33581e0657a10d567c6cfaa529521b34e20a39c9a29550698cbf252fabfa.svg)

![](images/f8/f84b296319e078df1827fe29dbd15fb61ce0d10cac69660f11d6a96d5c44478a.png)

Any given representation of a residue class is not unique.

For example, the integers congruent to zero modulo ![](images/f5/f5f3224583db57b9cfe323c8489ef5e5271000002b5ea253eb98fd067a858b2d.svg) are usually denoted ![](images/7e/7e03abb8339cac8bc90200b99c4de9c414e179036e7b7defca80f7388c9fdb7c.svg) In this case, ![](images/15/156b31ede73de5301befe67f02745a0202f1806a62f9fdecc6fc9ee3f21117ba.svg) is the **representative** of the class:
![](images/5f/5f298c564c0538edb6fc85abb585f5fef0b0bcff7fa704860794bb5681fb036d.svg)

However, we can use *any* element of the class to represent the class. Here are some examples:

![](images/38/383a513e20a70007e3d102dd4c8e9898550ac30514a3352842e1b9be8ad7601e.svg)

We can also use negative numbers as representatives of the class:

![](images/01/014ec5b5f21d3b216343811bddb6d84c3a66c7b29baa09504d67cab71b83aea6.svg)

What's important to understand is that *all of these sets are equal*:

![](images/31/3155c29054f13a2b96de8be909ebd1ac6c98d50f64ea5d7a0acef3f1dcf48ac1.svg)

The same idea is true for ![](images/7a/7ac9fdeb690307bfa97c781ae9ace4d91bbf6f3b15cfe6dd7139225bdca44fc5.svg)

![](images/cd/cd1101d39e228d23c551fcaa8ba377cd819661aaec6121706eab184658d2a854.svg)

The same idea applies to any residue class modulo ![](images/c2/c2475d72e6ec36042292de6c0160930174172b2386148d823a70e59fddfb93c2.svg) For example:

![](images/0c/0c4d211a3b3f6238f9e647585d62904af4fd263fb79eb94e45e9b51d8b62abde.svg)

Despite this non-uniqueness, we usually choose the smallest nonnegative element of a residue class to represent the class." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186153459 :tutorial/content "Let's list some important properties of residue classes:

- There are exactly $n$ *distinct* residue classes modulo $n.$

- If $a \equiv b \: (\text{mod}\:n)$ then $[a]_n=[b]_n.$ In particular, this allows us to pick any element of a class as its representative.

- On the other hand, two distinct residue classes have an empty intersection: 

$$
a \not\equiv b \quad (\text{mod}\:n)
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
[a]_n \cap [b]_n = \emptyset
$$

- The residue classes modulo $n$ form a partition of the set of all integers. This means the integers can be constructed from the (disjoint) union of all distinct residue classes. 

$$
\mathbb{Z} = [0]_n \cup [1]_n \cup \cdots \cup [n-1]_n
$$

The **integers modulo** $\boldsymbol n$ is defined as the set containing all distinct residue classes modulo $n$: 

$$
\mathbb{Z}_n = \big\{[0]_n,\, [1]_n,\, \ldots,\,  [n-1]_n\big\}
$$

The set $\mathbb Z_n$ has some interesting properties. We'll learn more about those in future lessons." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186152339 :activity/expected-seconds 540.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

- $[-1]_3$

- $[1]_3$" :question/worked-solution "We have $7 \in [a]_{3}$ if 

$$
7 \equiv a \quad (\text{mod}\:3).
$$

Let's now consider each of the given equivalence classes.

- $7 \in [4]_3$ because $7 \equiv 4 \: (\text{mod}\:3)$ $\quad \color{green}\checkmark$

- $7 \not\in [-1]_3$ because $7 \not\equiv -1 \: (\text{mod}\:3)$ $\quad \color{red}\times$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186152099 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-6ec8e64f-343c-590b-a372-9757c285ca4e" "question-c46ee0cd-65d1-59a8-92bc-e1fc2e8dbb10" "question-0c2846ce-57fa-59ad-9fe2-ab1c6ed9c653" "question-1bd78006-ade4-5556-a33a-5b5262685fbe" "question-06e706ec-ef55-5e4d-a1fb-e7ced3a44078"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186151848 :question/problem "If $[a]_n$ denotes the residue class containing all integers congruent to $a$ modulo $n,$ then which of the following residue classes is equal to $[13]_3?$

- $[0]_3$

- $[1]_3$

- $[2]_3$" :question/worked-solution "We have $[a]_{3} = [b]_{3}$ if 

$$
a \equiv b \quad (\text{mod}\:3).
$$

The residue class $[13]_{3}$ consists of the elements that are congruent to $13$ modulo $3.$ 

We can find an alternative representation for this residue class as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[13]_{3} & ={x\in Z\,|\,x≡13\,(\text{mod}\,3)} \\  & ={x\in Z\,|\,x≡4\cdot 3+1\,(\text{mod}\,3)} \\  & ={x\in Z\,|\,x≡4\cdot 0+1\,(\text{mod}\,3)} \\  & ={x\in Z\,|\,x≡1\,(\text{mod}\,3)} \\  & =[1]_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only"." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186152100 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-f68491fc-7fbf-551d-bb56-21bac80c159f" "question-0f9012f2-83ba-5f6f-b553-2ea47d5d4f81" "question-b83f0a5d-69e2-5527-92eb-107f538fccca" "question-32f1fbfd-ebfc-5a37-bf9e-b69da2b29724" "question-82a421fb-21ef-5dca-a27b-abed22994846"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186151850 :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true?

- There are $4$ distinct residue classes modulo $8$

- $[5]_{3} \cap [9]_{3} = \emptyset$

- $\mathbb{Z} = [4]_{3} \cup [5]_{3} \cup [9]_{3}$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the residue classes modulo $n$ have the following properties:

- There are exactly $n$ distinct residue classes modulo $n$

- Two distinct residue classes have an empty intersection: $[a]_n \cap [b]_n = \emptyset$ if $a \not\equiv b \: (\text{mod}\:n)$

- Residue classes modulo $n$ form a partition of the set of all integers: 

$$
\mathbb{Z} = [0]_n \cup [1]_n \cup \cdots \cup [n-1]_n
$$

- The integers modulo $n$ is defined as the set containing all distinct residue classes modulo $n$: 

$$
\mathbb{Z}_n = \big\{[0]_n,\, [1]_n,\, \ldots,\,  [n-1]_n\big\}
$$

With that in mind, let's now consider each of the given statements.

- Statement I is false. There are exactly $8$ distinct residue classes modulo $8.$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, since $5 \not\equiv 9 \: (\text{mod }3),$ we have that $[5]_3\cap [9]_3= \emptyset.$

- Statement III is true. First, notice the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}[4]_{3} & =[1+3\cdot 1]_{3}=[1]_{3} \\ [5]_{3} & =[2+3\cdot 1]_{3}=[2]_{3} \\ [9]_{3} & =[0+3\cdot 3]_{3}=[0]_{3}\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}[4]_{3}\cup [5]_{3}\cup [9]_{3} & =[1]_{3}\cup [2]_{3}\cup [0]_{3} \\  & =[0]_{3}\cup [1]_{3}\cup [2]_{3} \\  & =Z.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only"." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-e91f8fe9-c6f2-558a-bf39-b0389019d5ff" :question/id #uuid "e91f8fe9-c6f2-558a-bf39-b0389019d5ff" :question/math-academy-id "q-86021" :question/problem "Which of the following integers belong to the residue class $[7]_{11}?$

- There are $11$ distinct residue classes modulo $11$
- $[7]_{5}\cap [2]_{5}\ne ∅$
- $Z=[0]_{4}\cup [9]_{4}\cup [2]_{4}\cup [15]_{4}$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the residue classes modulo $n$ have the following properties:

- There are exactly $n$ distinct residue classes modulo $n$

- Two distinct residue classes have an empty intersection: $[a]_{n}\cap [b]_{n}=∅$ if $a≢b\,(\text{mod}\,n)$

- Residue classes modulo $n$ form a partition of the set of all integers: 

$$
Z=[0]_{n}\cup [1]_{n}\cup ⋯\cup [n-1]_{n}
$$

- The integers modulo $n$ is defined as the set containing all distinct residue classes modulo $n$: 

$$
{Z}_{n}={[0]_{n},\,[1]_{n},\,…,\,[n-1]_{n}}
$$

With that in mind, let's now consider each of the given statements.

- Statement I is true. There are $11$ distinct residue classes modulo $11.$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, since $7≡2\,(\text{mod }5),$ we have that $[7]_{5}=[2]_{5}.$ Therefore, $[7]_{5}\cap [2]_{5}\ne ∅.$

- Statement III is true. First, notice the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}[9]_{4} & =[1+4\cdot 2]_{4}=[1]_{4} \\ [15]_{4} & =[3+4\cdot 3]_{4}=[3]_{4}\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}[0]_{4}\cup [9]_{4}\cup [2]_{4}\cup [15]_{4} & =[0]_{4}\cup [1]_{4}\cup [2]_{4}\cup [3]_{4} \\  & =Z\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III"." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-0dd3a9af-e1c5-54e0-8441-f550817b9384"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-0dd3a9af-e1c5-54e0-8441-f550817b9384" :answer-field/id #uuid "0dd3a9af-e1c5-54e0-8441-f550817b9384" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-ccfb74cf-ee0e-514f-afc8-cbb35b8f9393" :answer-field/choices ["answer-52eadcaf-a11c-568b-907e-2ff81396dc49" "answer-406d20f8-1407-5435-8784-5f3e29ff681c" "answer-7ecfdc45-6d9f-55e1-936c-36ea7836a224" "answer-ccfb74cf-ee0e-514f-afc8-cbb35b8f9393" "answer-4a92891f-39e5-5cee-b46a-8784882f23fc"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-52eadcaf-a11c-568b-907e-2ff81396dc49" :answer/id #uuid "52eadcaf-a11c-568b-907e-2ff81396dc49" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-406d20f8-1407-5435-8784-5f3e29ff681c" :answer/id #uuid "406d20f8-1407-5435-8784-5f3e29ff681c" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7ecfdc45-6d9f-55e1-936c-36ea7836a224" :answer/id #uuid "7ecfdc45-6d9f-55e1-936c-36ea7836a224" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ccfb74cf-ee0e-514f-afc8-cbb35b8f9393" :answer/id #uuid "ccfb74cf-ee0e-514f-afc8-cbb35b8f9393" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I, II, and III" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4a92891f-39e5-5cee-b46a-8784882f23fc" :answer/id #uuid "4a92891f-39e5-5cee-b46a-8784882f23fc" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-0f9012f2-83ba-5f6f-b553-2ea47d5d4f81" :question/id #uuid "0f9012f2-83ba-5f6f-b553-2ea47d5d4f81" :question/math-academy-id "q-78640" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true?

"{[0]_{11},[1]_{11},…,[10]_{11}}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186153456 :tutorial/content "Given an integer $a,$ the **residue class** (or **congruence class**) of $a$ modulo $n$ is the set containing all integers congruent to $a$ (modulo $n$). 

The residue class of $a$ modulo $n,$ denoted $[a]_n,$ can be expressed using a conditional definition as follows:

$$
[a]_n = \big\{ x \in \mathbb{Z} \: | \: x \equiv a \,  \: (\text{mod}\:n) \big\}
$$

Put another way, the residue class $[a]_n$ contains all integers that have the same remainder as $a$ when divided by $n.$

For example, the residue class of $0$ modulo $2$ contains all the even integers because they all have a remainder of zero when divided by $2.$

$$
\begin{aligned}[0]_{2} & ={x\in Z\,|\,x≡0\,(\text{mod}\,2)} \\  & ={2k\,|\,k\in Z} \\  & ={…,-4,-2,0,2,4…}\end{aligned}
$$

The residue class of $1$ modulo $2$ contains all the odd integers because they all have a remainder of one when divided by $2.$

$$
\begin{aligned}[1]_{2} & ={x\in Z\,|\,x≡1\,(\text{mod}\,2)} \\  & ={2k+1\,|\,k\in Z} \\  & ={…,-3,-1,1,3,5…}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that each element of $\mathbb Z$ lies either in $[0]_2$ or in $[1]_2$ (but never both). Thus, these residue classes form a *partition* of the integers. We'll call this partition $\mathbb Z_2{:}$

$$
\mathbb Z_2 = \big\{[0]_2, [1]_2\big\}
$$

We can visualize this partition using the diagram shown below.

![](images/f8/f84b296319e078df1827fe29dbd15fb61ce0d10cac69660f11d6a96d5c44478a.png)

Similarly, the integers can also be partitioned into five residue classes modulo $5.$ 

$$
\mathbb Z_5 = \big\{[0]_5, [1]_5, [2]_5,[3]_5, [4]_5 \big\}
$$

In this case, each residue class contains all numbers that are congruent modulo $5.$ We can visualize this partition of $\mathbb Z$ using the diagram below.

![](images/27/270f63afd4a0022e9f31a48e5ea5f4e799822e8c4eb5813e6c5e616e316c02e1.png)

A residue class is a specific type of a more general object called an **equivalence class.** We'll learn more about different types of equivalence classes soon." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186153479 :tutorial/content "Let's go back to our diagram for visualizing the residue classes modulo ![](images/27/270d33581e0657a10d567c6cfaa529521b34e20a39c9a29550698cbf252fabfa.svg)

![](images/f8/f84b296319e078df1827fe29dbd15fb61ce0d10cac69660f11d6a96d5c44478a.png)

Any given representation of a residue class is not unique.

For example, the integers congruent to zero modulo ![](images/f5/f5f3224583db57b9cfe323c8489ef5e5271000002b5ea253eb98fd067a858b2d.svg) are usually denoted ![](images/7e/7e03abb8339cac8bc90200b99c4de9c414e179036e7b7defca80f7388c9fdb7c.svg) In this case, ![](images/15/156b31ede73de5301befe67f02745a0202f1806a62f9fdecc6fc9ee3f21117ba.svg) is the **representative** of the class:
![](images/5f/5f298c564c0538edb6fc85abb585f5fef0b0bcff7fa704860794bb5681fb036d.svg)

However, we can use *any* element of the class to represent the class. Here are some examples:

![](images/38/383a513e20a70007e3d102dd4c8e9898550ac30514a3352842e1b9be8ad7601e.svg)

We can also use negative numbers as representatives of the class:

![](images/01/014ec5b5f21d3b216343811bddb6d84c3a66c7b29baa09504d67cab71b83aea6.svg)

What's important to understand is that *all of these sets are equal*:

![](images/31/3155c29054f13a2b96de8be909ebd1ac6c98d50f64ea5d7a0acef3f1dcf48ac1.svg)

The same idea is true for ![](images/7a/7ac9fdeb690307bfa97c781ae9ace4d91bbf6f3b15cfe6dd7139225bdca44fc5.svg)

![](images/cd/cd1101d39e228d23c551fcaa8ba377cd819661aaec6121706eab184658d2a854.svg)

The same idea applies to any residue class modulo ![](images/c2/c2475d72e6ec36042292de6c0160930174172b2386148d823a70e59fddfb93c2.svg) For example:

![](images/0c/0c4d211a3b3f6238f9e647585d62904af4fd263fb79eb94e45e9b51d8b62abde.svg)

Despite this non-uniqueness, we usually choose the smallest nonnegative element of a residue class to represent the class." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186153459 :tutorial/content "Let's list some important properties of residue classes:

- There are exactly $n$ *distinct* residue classes modulo $n.$

- If $a \equiv b \: (\text{mod}\:n)$ then $[a]_n=[b]_n.$ In particular, this allows us to pick any element of a class as its representative.

- On the other hand, two distinct residue classes have an empty intersection: 

$$
a \not\equiv b \quad (\text{mod}\:n)
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
[a]_n \cap [b]_n = \emptyset
$$

- The residue classes modulo $n$ form a partition of the set of all integers. This means the integers can be constructed from the (disjoint) union of all distinct residue classes. 

$$
\mathbb{Z} = [0]_n \cup [1]_n \cup \cdots \cup [n-1]_n
$$

The **integers modulo** $\boldsymbol n$ is defined as the set containing all distinct residue classes modulo $n$: 

$$
\mathbb{Z}_n = \big\{[0]_n,\, [1]_n,\, \ldots,\,  [n-1]_n\big\}
$$

The set $\mathbb Z_n$ has some interesting properties. We'll learn more about those in future lessons." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186152339 :activity/expected-seconds 540.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}] "assertions" [[17592186151846 :question/problem "Which of the following integers belong to the residue class $[5]_{8}?$

- $-12$
- $3$
- $24$"] [17592186152792 :question/worked-solution "The residue class $[6]_{9}$ consists of the elements that are congruent to $6$ modulo $9.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}[6]_{9} & ={x\in Z\,|\,x≡6\,(\text{mod}\,9)} \\  & ={x\in Z\,|\,x=6+9k,\,k\in Z} \\  & ={6+9k\,|\,k\in Z} \\  & ={…,\,6-2\cdot 9,\,6-9,\,6,\,6+9,\,6+2\cdot 9,\,…} \\  & ={…,-12,-3,6,15,24,…}.\end{aligned}
$$

We see that $-12$ and $24$ belong to $[6]_{9},$ while $3$ does not.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only"."] [17592186152792 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-cce84edd-038c-58d1-9051-41a39c1a5bad" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-f68491fc-7fbf-551d-bb56-21bac80c159f" :question/math-academy-id "q-78644"] ["question-f68491fc-7fbf-551d-bb56-21bac80c159f" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true?

- There are $11$ distinct residue classes modulo $11$
- $[7]_{5}\cap [2]_{5}\ne ∅$
- $Z=[0]_{4}\cup [9]_{4}\cup [2]_{4}\cup [15]_{4}$"] ["question-f68491fc-7fbf-551d-bb56-21bac80c159f" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the residue classes modulo $n$ have the following properties:

- There are exactly $n$ distinct residue classes modulo $n$

- Two distinct residue classes have an empty intersection: $[a]_{n}\cap [b]_{n}=∅$ if $a≢b\,(\text{mod}\,n)$

- Residue classes modulo $n$ form a partition of the set of all integers: 

$$
Z=[0]_{n}\cup [1]_{n}\cup ⋯\cup [n-1]_{n}
$$

- The integers modulo $n$ is defined as the set containing all distinct residue classes modulo $n$: 

$$
{Z}_{n}={[0]_{n},\,[1]_{n},\,…,\,[n-1]_{n}}
$$

With that in mind, let's now consider each of the given statements.

- Statement I is true. There are $11$ distinct residue classes modulo $11.$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, since $7≡2\,(\text{mod }5),$ we have that $[7]_{5}=[2]_{5}.$ Therefore, $[7]_{5}\cap [2]_{5}\ne ∅.$

- Statement III is true. First, notice the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}[9]_{4} & =[1+4\cdot 2]_{4}=[1]_{4} \\ [15]_{4} & =[3+4\cdot 3]_{4}=[3]_{4}\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}[0]_{4}\cup [9]_{4}\cup [2]_{4}\cup [15]_{4} & =[0]_{4}\cup [1]_{4}\cup [2]_{4}\cup [3]_{4} \\  & =Z\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III"."] ["question-f68491fc-7fbf-551d-bb56-21bac80c159f" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true?

- $[5]_{3}\cap [1]_{3}\ne ∅$

- Residue classes modulo $n$ form a partition of the set of all integers: 

$$
Z=[0]_{n}\cup [1]_{n}\cup ⋯\cup [n-1]_{n}
$$

- The integers modulo $n$ is defined as the set containing all distinct residue classes modulo $n$: 

$$
{Z}_{n}={[0]_{n},\,[1]_{n},\,…,\,[n-1]_{n}}
$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}[3]_{2}\cup [6]_{2} & =[1]_{2}\cup [0]_{2} \\  & =[0]_{2}\cup [1]_{2} \\  & =Z\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only"."] ["question-0f9012f2-83ba-5f6f-b553-2ea47d5d4f81" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-2372040f-636b-51db-a88a-0a20d411e932" $$

$$
{Z}_{n}={[0]_{n},\,[1]_{n},\,…,\,[n-1]_{n}}
$$

$$

"answer-field-fd3fc3a4-ac23-58a2-9227-8ac4db6385c8"] [17592186152100 :knowledge-point/questions "question-82a421fb-21ef-5dca-a27b-abed22994846"] [17592186153456 :tutorial/content "Given an integer $a,$ the **residue class** (or **congruence class**) of $a$ modulo $n$ is the set containing all integers congruent to $a$ (modulo $n$). 

The residue class of $a$ modulo $n,$ denoted $[a]_n,$ can be expressed using a conditional definition as follows:

$$
[a]_n = \big\{ x \in \mathbb{Z} \: | \: x \equiv a \,  \: (\text{mod}\:n) \big\}
$$

Put another way, the residue class $[a]_n$ contains all integers that have the same remainder as $a$ when divided by $n.$

For example, the residue class of $0$ modulo $2$ contains all the even integers because they all have a remainder of zero when divided by $2.$

$$
\begin{aligned}[0]_{2} & ={x\in Z\,|\,x≡0\,(\text{mod}\,2)} \\  & ={2k\,|\,k\in Z} \\  & ={…,-4,-2,0,2,4…}\end{aligned}
$$

The residue class of $1$ modulo $2$ contains all the odd integers because they all have a remainder of one when divided by $2.$

$$
\begin{aligned}[1]_{2} & ={x\in Z\,|\,x≡1\,(\text{mod}\,2)} \\  & ={2k+1\,|\,k\in Z} \\  & ={…,-3,-1,1,3,5…}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that each element of $\mathbb Z$ lies either in $[0]_2$ or in $[1]_2$ (but never both). Thus, these residue classes form a *partition* of the integers. We'll call this partition $\mathbb Z_2{:}$

$$
\mathbb Z_2 = \big\{[0]_2, [1]_2\big\}
$$

We can visualize this partition using the diagram shown below.

![](images/f8/f84b296319e078df1827fe29dbd15fb61ce0d10cac69660f11d6a96d5c44478a.png)

Similarly, the integers can also be partitioned into five residue classes modulo $5.$ 

$$
\mathbb Z_5 = \big\{[0]_5, [1]_5, [2]_5,[3]_5, [4]_5 \big\}
$$

In this case, each residue class contains all numbers that are congruent modulo $5.$ We can visualize this partition of $\mathbb Z$ using the diagram below.

![](images/27/270f63afd4a0022e9f31a48e5ea5f4e799822e8c4eb5813e6c5e616e316c02e1.png)

A residue class is a specific type of a more general object called an **equivalence class.** We'll learn more about different types of equivalence classes soon."] [17592186153479 :tutorial/content "Let's go back to our diagram for visualizing the residue classes modulo ![](images/27/270d33581e0657a10d567c6cfaa529521b34e20a39c9a29550698cbf252fabfa.svg)

![](images/f8/f84b296319e078df1827fe29dbd15fb61ce0d10cac69660f11d6a96d5c44478a.png)

Any given representation of a residue class is not unique.

For example, the integers congruent to zero modulo ![](images/f5/f5f3224583db57b9cfe323c8489ef5e5271000002b5ea253eb98fd067a858b2d.svg) are usually denoted ![](images/7e/7e03abb8339cac8bc90200b99c4de9c414e179036e7b7defca80f7388c9fdb7c.svg) In this case, ![](images/15/156b31ede73de5301befe67f02745a0202f1806a62f9fdecc6fc9ee3f21117ba.svg) is the **representative** of the class:
![](images/5f/5f298c564c0538edb6fc85abb585f5fef0b0bcff7fa704860794bb5681fb036d.svg)

Despite this non-uniqueness, we usually choose the smallest nonnegative element of a residue class to represent the class."] [17592186153459 :tutorial/content "Let's list some important properties of residue classes:

- There are exactly $n$ *distinct* residue classes modulo $n.$

- If $a \equiv b \: (\text{mod}\:n)$ then $[a]_n=[b]_n.$ In particular, this allows us to pick any element of a class as its representative.

- On the other hand, two distinct residue classes have an empty intersection: 

$$
a \not\equiv b \quad (\text{mod}\:n)
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
[a]_n \cap [b]_n = \emptyset
$$

- The residue classes modulo $n$ form a partition of the set of all integers. This means the integers can be constructed from the (disjoint) union of all distinct residue classes. 

$$
\mathbb{Z} = [0]_n \cup [1]_n \cup \cdots \cup [n-1]_n
$$

The **integers modulo** $\boldsymbol n$ is defined as the set containing all distinct residue classes modulo $n$: 

$$
\mathbb{Z}_n = \big\{[0]_n,\, [1]_n,\, \ldots,\,  [n-1]_n\big\}
$$

The set $\mathbb Z_n$ has some interesting properties. We'll learn more about those in future lessons."] [17592186152339 :activity/expected-seconds 540.0]] "retractions" [[17592186151846 :question/problem "Which of the following integers belong to the residue class $[5]_{8}$?

$$
[a]_n = \big\{x \in \mathbb{Z} \: \mid \: x \equiv a \, \: (\text{mod}\:n) \big\}

$$
\begin{aligned}

\end{aligned}
$$

class** (or **congruence class**) of $a$ modulo $n$ is the set containing all integers congruent to $a$ (modulo $n$).

The residue class of $a$ modulo $n$, denoted $[a]_n$, can be expressed using a conditional definition as follows:

$$
[a]_n = \big\{x \in \mathbb{Z} \: \mid \: x \equiv a \, \: (\text{mod}\:n) \big\}
$$

Put another way, the residue class $[a]_n$ contains all integers that have the same remainder as $a$ when divided by $n$.

For example, the residue class of $0$ modulo $2$ contains all the even integers because they all have a remainder of zero when divided by $2$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
[0]_{2} &= {x ∈ Z\begin{vmatrix}x≡0(mod2)} \\ = {2k\end{vmatrix}k ∈ Z} \\
&= {…,-4,-2, 0, 2, 4…}
\end{aligned}
$$

The residue class of $1$ modulo $2$ contains all the odd integers because they all have a remainder of one when divided by $2$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
[1]_{2} &= {x ∈ Z\begin{vmatrix}x≡1(mod2)} \\ = {2k + 1\end{vmatrix}k ∈ Z} \\
&= {…,-3,-1, 1, 3, 5…}
\end{aligned}
$$

Note that each element of $\mathbb Z$ lies either in $[0]_2$ or in $[1]_2$ (but never both). Thus, these residue classes form a *partition* of the integers. We'll call this partition $\mathbb Z_2{:}$

$$
\mathbb Z_2 = \big\{[0]_2, [1]_2\big\}
$$

We can visualize this partition using the diagram shown below.

![](images/f8/f84b296319e078df1827fe29dbd15fb61ce0d10cac69660f11d6a96d5c44478a.png)

Similarly, the integers can also be partitioned into five residue classes modulo $5$.

$$
\mathbb Z_5 = \big\{[0]_5, [1]_5, [2]_5,[3]_5, [4]_5 \big\}
$$

In this case, each residue class contains all numbers that are congruent modulo $5$. We can visualize this partition of $\mathbb Z$ using the diagram below.

![](images/27/270f63afd4a0022e9f31a48e5ea5f4e799822e8c4eb5813e6c5e616e316c02e1.png)

A residue class is a specific type of a more general object called an **equivalence class.** We'll learn more about different types of equivalence classes soon." :tutorial/id #uuid "26e8368d-0ec3-5b4d-8487-94376b8840d7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9028 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "257362f2-5f70-5a26-bc18-e59dfebb619c" :step/math-academy-id 156895 :step/next {:db/id 17592186152964}} {:db/id 17592186152964 :step/content {:db/id 17592186153479 :tutorial/content "Let's go back to our diagram for visualizing the residue classes modulo $2$.

![](images/f8/f84b296319e078df1827fe29dbd15fb61ce0d10cac69660f11d6a96d5c44478a.png)

Any given representation of a residue class is not unique.

For example, the integers congruent to zero modulo $2$ are usually denoted $[0]_2$. In this case, $0$ is the **representative** of the class:

$$
[0]_{2} = {x \mid x≡0(mod2)}
$$

However, we can use *any* element of the class to represent the class. Here are some examples:

$$
\begin{aligned}
[2]_{2} &= {x\begin{vmatrix}x≡2(mod2)} \\ [4]_{2}|= {x \mid x≡4(mod2)} \\ [6]_{2}|= {x\end{vmatrix}x≡6(mod2)} \\
&= ⋮
\end{aligned}
$$

We can also use negative numbers as representatives of the class:

$$
\begin{aligned}
[- 2]_{2} &= {x\begin{vmatrix}x≡ - 2(mod2)} \\ [- 4]_{2}|= {x \mid x≡ - 4(mod2)} \\ [- 6]_{2}|= {x\end{vmatrix}x≡ - 6(mod2)} \\
&= ⋮
\end{aligned}
$$

What's important to understand is that *all of these sets are equal*:

$$
\begin{aligned}
[0]_{2} &= [2]_{2} = [4]_{2} = [6]_{2} = ⋯ \\
&= [- 2]_{2} = [- 4]_{2} = [- 6]_{2} = ⋯
\end{aligned}
$$

The same idea is true for $[1]_2{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
[1]_{2} &= [3]_{2} = [5]_{2} = [7]_{2} = ⋯ \\
&= [- 1]_{2} = [- 3]_{2} = [- 5]_{2} = ⋯
\end{aligned}
$$

The same idea applies to any residue class modulo $n$. For example:

$$
\begin{aligned}
[0]_{5} &= [5]_{5} = [10]_{5} = ⋯ \\
[1]_{5} &= [6]_{5} = [11]_{5} = ⋯ \\
[2]_{5} &= [7]_{5} = [12]_{5} = ⋯ \\
[3]_{5} &= [8]_{5} = [13]_{5} = ⋯ \\
[4]_{5} &= [9]_{5} = [15]_{5} = ⋯
\end{aligned}
$$

Despite this non-uniqueness, we usually choose the smallest nonnegative element of a residue class to represent the class." :tutorial/id #uuid "24c78443-01dd-5900-a2c6-3d43b549b1b3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9215 :tutorial/title "Representatives"} :step/id #uuid "92e60d57-6f02-556f-bc8c-58071a44c310" :step/math-academy-id 156896 :step/next {:db/id 17592186152965}} {:db/id 17592186152965 :step/content {:db/id 17592186152097 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186151846 :question/id #uuid "41276052-e364-593e-9557-5d645f169a74" :question/math-academy-id "e-14600"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "3d2f207a-8e99-5520-ab9f-266c8f54465b" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049004} {:db/id 17592186050035}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186152787} {:db/id 17592186152792}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Elements Belonging to a Residue Class"} :step/id #uuid "c6e19ef8-a2b2-5b43-8bef-8b33d3e37a4d" :step/math-academy-id 156897 :step/next {:db/id 17592186152966}} {:db/id 17592186152966 :step/content {:db/id 17592186152098 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186151847 :question/id #uuid "33da67df-113b-58e2-ad3e-a45d1568d75d" :question/math-academy-id "e-14601"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "9c1fe7ea-d91e-5440-b756-37a460a18f19" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186152788} {:db/id 17592186152793}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Residue Classes Containing a Given Element"} :step/id #uuid "bf05b2fd-4901-5647-b876-8df098ff47f5" :step/math-academy-id 156900 :step/next {:db/id 17592186152967}} {:db/id 17592186152967 :step/content {:db/id 17592186153459 :tutorial/content "Let's list some important properties of residue classes:

The **integers modulo** $\boldsymbol n$ is defined as the set containing all distinct residue classes modulo $n$:

$$

- There are exactly $n$ *distinct* residue classes modulo $n$.
- If $a \equiv b \: (\text{mod}\:n)$ then $[a]_n=[b]_n$. In particular, this allows us to pick any element of a class as its representative.
- On the other hand, two distinct residue classes have an empty intersection:
$a \not\equiv b \quad (\text{mod}\:n) \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad [a]_n \cap [b]_n = \emptyset$
- The residue classes modulo $n$ form a partition of the set of all integers. This means the integers can be constructed from the (disjoint) union of all distinct residue classes.
$\mathbb{Z} = [0]_n \cup [1]_n \cup \cdots \cup [n-1]_n$

The **integers modulo** $\boldsymbol n$ is defined as the set containing all distinct residue classes modulo $n$:

$$
\mathbb{Z}_n = \big\{[0]_n,\, [1]_n,\, \ldots,\, [n-1]_n\big\}
$$

and constructing formal mathematical arguments. Students will formalize their understanding of logic, sets, and functions while delving into new concepts such as congruence, relations, and cardinality.
This course serves as ideal preparation for students wishing to pursue undergraduate studies in formal mathematical disciplines, including Discrete Mathematics, Abstract Algebra, and Real Analysis.

A robust knowledge of set theory is another cornerstone of mathematical proof-writing. Students will extend and formalize their understanding of sets and learn to translate between logical and set operations. By the end of the course, students will appreciate how set theory provides a comprehensive toolkit for proving mathematical results.
After mastering these fundamentals, students will explore various proof-writing techniques, including direct proof, proof by cases, proof by contrapositive, proof by contradiction, disproof, and mathematical induction. The course emphasizes proving concepts related to parity, divisibility, congruence, sequences, functions, set identities, and relations. Students will have multiple opportunities to test and refine their proof construction and comprehension skills throughout the course and in varied contexts
This challenging yet engaging course helps students with strong mathematical foundations build a solid base for further progression into advanced undergraduate courses." 17592186045417] The residue class of $a$ modulo $n$, denoted $[a]_n$, can be expressed using a conditional definition as follows:

$$
[a]_n = \big\{x \in \mathbb{Z} \: \mid \: x \equiv a \, \: (\text{mod}\:n) \big\}
$$

Put another way, the residue class $[a]_n$ contains all integers that have the same remainder as $a$ when divided by $n$.

For example, the residue class of $0$ modulo $2$ contains all the even integers because they all have a remainder of zero when divided by $2$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
[0]_{2} &= {x ∈ Z\begin{vmatrix}x≡0(mod2)} \\ = {2k\end{vmatrix}k ∈ Z} \\
&= {…,-4,-2, 0, 2, 4…}
\end{aligned}
$$

The residue class of $1$ modulo $2$ contains all the odd integers because they all have a remainder of one when divided by $2$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
[1]_{2} &= {x ∈ Z\begin{vmatrix}x≡1(mod2)} \\ = {2k + 1\end{vmatrix}k ∈ Z} \\
&= {…,-3,-1, 1, 3, 5…}
\end{aligned}
$$

Note that each element of $\mathbb Z$ lies either in $[0]_2$ or in $[1]_2$ (but never both). Thus, these residue classes form a *partition* of the integers. We'll call this partition $\mathbb Z_2{:}$

$$
\mathbb Z_2 = \big\{[0]_2, [1]_2\big\}
$$

We can visualize this partition using the diagram shown below.

![](images/f8/f84b296319e078df1827fe29dbd15fb61ce0d10cac69660f11d6a96d5c44478a.png)

Similarly, the integers can also be partitioned into five residue classes modulo $5$.

$$
\mathbb Z_5 = \big\{[0]_5, [1]_5, [2]_5,[3]_5, [4]_5 \big\}
$$

In this case, each residue class contains all numbers that are congruent modulo $5$. We can visualize this partition of $\mathbb Z$ using the diagram below.

![](images/27/270f63afd4a0022e9f31a48e5ea5f4e799822e8c4eb5813e6c5e616e316c02e1.png)

A residue class is a specific type of a more general object called an **equivalence class.** We'll learn more about different types of equivalence classes soon." 17592186045417] [17592186153456 1065 9028 17592186045417] [17592186153456 1066 #uuid "26e8368d-0ec3-5b4d-8487-94376b8840d7" 17592186045417] [17592186153456 1067 "Introduction" 17592186045417] [17592186153459 1064 "Let's list some important properties of residue classes:

- There are exactly $n$ *distinct* residue classes modulo $n$.
- If $a \equiv b \: (\text{mod}\:n)$ then $[a]_n=[b]_n$. In particular, this allows us to pick any element of a class as its representative.
- On the other hand, two distinct residue classes have an empty intersection:
$a \not\equiv b \quad (\text{mod}\:n) \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad [a]_n \cap [b]_n = \emptyset$
- The residue classes modulo $n$ form a partition of the set of all integers. This means the integers can be constructed from the (disjoint) union of all distinct residue classes.
$\mathbb{Z} = [0]_n \cup [1]_n \cup \cdots \cup [n-1]_n$

The **integers modulo** $\boldsymbol n$ is defined as the set containing all distinct residue classes modulo $n$:

$$
\mathbb{Z}_n = \big\{[0]_n,\, [1]_n,\, \ldots,\, [n-1]_n\big\}
$$

The set $\mathbb Z_n$ has some interesting properties. Any given representation of a residue class is not unique.

For example, the integers congruent to zero modulo $2$ are usually denoted $[0]_2$. In this case, $0$ is the **representative** of the class:

$$
[0]_{2} = {x \mid x≡0(mod2)}
$$

However, we can use *any* element of the class to represent the class. Here are some examples:

$$
\begin{aligned}
[2]_{2} &= {x\begin{vmatrix}x≡2(mod2)} \\ [4]_{2}|= {x \mid x≡4(mod2)} \\ [6]_{2}|= {x\end{vmatrix}x≡6(mod2)} \\
&= ⋮
\end{aligned}
$$

We can also use negative numbers as representatives of the class:

$$
\begin{aligned}
[- 2]_{2} &= {x\begin{vmatrix}x≡ - 2(mod2)} \\ [- 4]_{2}|= {x \mid x≡ - 4(mod2)} \\ [- 6]_{2}|= {x\end{vmatrix}x≡ - 6(mod2)} \\
&= ⋮
\end{aligned}
$$

What's important to understand is that *all of these sets are equal*:

$$
\begin{aligned}
[0]_{2} &= [2]_{2} = [4]_{2} = [6]_{2} = ⋯ \\
&= [- 2]_{2} = [- 4]_{2} = [- 6]_{2} = ⋯
\end{aligned}
$$

The same idea is true for $[1]_2{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
[1]_{2} &= [3]_{2} = [5]_{2} = [7]_{2} = ⋯ \\
&= [- 1]_{2} = [- 3]_{2} = [- 5]_{2} = ⋯
\end{aligned}
$$

The same idea applies to any residue class modulo $n$. For example:

$$
\begin{aligned}
[0]_{5} &= [5]_{5} = [10]_{5} = ⋯ \\
[1]_{5} &= [6]_{5} = [11]_{5} = ⋯ \\
[2]_{5} &= [7]_{5} = [12]_{5} = ⋯ \\
[3]_{5} &= [8]_{5} = [13]_{5} = ⋯ \\
[4]_{5} &= [9]_{5} = [15]_{5} = ⋯
\end{aligned}
$$

Despite this non-uniqueness, we usually choose the smallest nonnegative element of a residue class to represent the class." 17592186045417] [17592186153479 1065 9215 17592186045417] [17592186153479 1066 #uuid "24c78443-01dd-5900-a2c6-3d43b549b1b3" 17592186045417] [17592186153479 1067 "Representatives" 17592186045417]]}
